newsitem.title: LEBANON: South Lebanon votes in key test to Hizbollah.
newsitem.headline: South Lebanon votes in key test to Hizbollah.

text.p: Voting proceeded peacefully in mainly Shi'ite Moslem south Lebanon on Sunday in the fourth round of Lebanon's parliamentary elections seen as a key test to the popularity of the pro-Iranian Hizbollah group.

Hizbollah, the main group fighting a guerrilla war to oust Israeli troops from south Lebanon, was seeking a political comeback, bidding to win four seats in the country's assembly after suffering losses in earlier rounds of voting.
Some 8,000 troops clamped heavy security on volatile south Lebanon where 552,000 voters were eligible to choose 23 deputies to the 128-member half-Christian, half-Moslem parliament.

Voting was brisk in the port of Sidon and the market town of Nabatiyeh but lighter in Tyre further south. Bearded men, and women in Iranian-style head-to-toe black chadors queued since early morning to cast their ballots in segregated booths.
The vote, and next Sunday's in the eastern Bekaa Valley, will decide the distribution of the majority of seats set for Lebanon's 1.3 million Shi'ites in the national assembly.

Polls closed at five p.m. (1400 GMT) without incident. Fears of violence at the ballot box were allayed after rival Shi'ite groups -- the secular Amal and Hizbollah (Party of God) -- buried the hatchet and joined forces in the polls.

Syria had forged an eleventh hour pact to run a joint Amal-Hizbollah list of candidates despite a history of enmity and a bitter war in late 1980s for supremacy of the Shi'ite community, Lebanon's largest religious group.
The joint ticket, headed by Amal chief Nabih Berri, the parliament speaker and a former civil war militia head, had five Amal and four Hizbollah candidates. The rest were Amal allies.

Amal and Hizbollah both had a strong showing during Sunday's vote. Dozens of cars carrying either yellow Hizbollah flags, showing a fist clutching an AK-47 assault rifle, or Amal's green flags drove through southern cities and villages.
The joint ticket does not nominate any candidates for two Sunni Moslem seats for the port of Sidon.

But Berri has urged supporters to vote for Bahia al-Hariri, sister of Prime Minister Rafik Hariri, and an ally. Hizbollah, a staunch foe of Hariri, said its followers would vote for two other candidates.

The prime minister declared electoral war on Hizbollah last month, calling the five-sage election a battle of moderation against extremism, and the militant group lost two parliamentary seats to government supporters in earlier rounds of voting.
Hizbollah had eight MPs and four allies in the outgoing parliament but appears unlikely to match that number in the current election.

Under the pact, Hizbollah will have three candidates and two supporters on another joint list in next Sunday's voting in the Bekaa. If all its candidates win, its representation in the new parliament will be reduced by one deputy and two supporters.
Two other lists running in the south were a 10-member leftist ticket and a 15-member list headed by Kamel Assad, a traditionalist politician and former parliament speaker.

A private watchdog group, the Lebanese Association for the Democracy of Elections, reported a drop in abuses during Sunday's vote compared to widespread violations in the three earlier rounds of voting.
It said police were illegally inside many polling stations, some of which lacked isolating curtains for voters to prepare lists in secret, and names were missing from voter lists.
